narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven first by your class ranking at the end of your third year, which placed you in the bottom decile. This was the single strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Your first-year ranking, also in the bottom decile, added further weight in the same direction. These two academic-standing measures outweighed everything else.

Your LSAT score of 36 worked mildly in your favor, pulling the prediction slightly toward passing, but it was not strong enough to overcome the impact of your low class rankings. Other details such as your undergraduate GPA of 2.5, upper-middle family income, gender, race, and full-time status played only minor roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-40s. Strengthening these two areas would most directly reduce your predicted risk of failing the bar exam. Consider reapplying once you have clearer evidence of stronger performance.
